1. Introduction & Pharmacology

Tintinalli Ch.177 p.1194
  • Cyclic antidepressants (CAs / TCAs) were the first generation of antidepressants developed.
  • Although largely supplanted by SSRIs/SNRIs, they remain prescribed for chronic pain, migraine prophylaxis, and refractory depression — and remain a major cause of severe poisoning fatality.
  • ~50% of CA exposures reported to US Poison Control Centers result in significant toxicity.
  • Toxic dose threshold: >1 g (or >15–20 mg/kg) can be lethal in adults; smaller in children.
  • Eight CAs commonly used in US — see Table 177-1 below.

Structure

  • Tertiary amines (e.g., amitriptyline, clomipramine, doxepin, imipramine, trimipramine): potent serotonin reuptake blockers.
  • Secondary amines (desipramine, nortriptyline, protriptyline): primarily norepinephrine reuptake blockers — generally less anticholinergic.
  • Tetracyclic: amoxapine, maprotiline.
  • Tertiary amines are demethylated to active secondary metabolites — toxicity persists beyond parent half-life.
📚 Table 177-1 — Cyclic Antidepressants and Related Drugs: typical dose, max dose, half-life, active metabolites (Tintinalli p.1195)

Pharmacokinetics

  • Absorption: rapid; peak plasma 2–8 h after therapeutic dose. Anticholinergic effects can delay absorption in overdose, prolonging the toxicity window.
  • Bioavailability: ~30–70% (significant first-pass).
  • Distribution: very large Vd (10–50 L/kg) — highly protein-bound, lipophilic.
  • Elimination: hepatic CYP450; long half-lives (~10 to >100 h).
  • Hemodialysis is NOT effective (high Vd + high protein binding).
Pearl — measurement: serum CA levels do not reliably correlate with clinical severity. Total parent + metabolite >1000 ng/mL associates with severe toxicity, but treatment is guided by clinical findings + ECG, not levels.
Inline MCQ 1. Which is the most reliable predictor of cyclic antidepressant toxicity severity?

Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
C. Time of last dose by history
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
D. Pupil size
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. ECG findings (especially QRS >100 ms and tall R in aVR) plus clinical status guide management. Levels are unreliable. Reference: Tintinalli p.1196.

2. Mechanisms of Toxicity

Tintinalli Tables 177-2 & 177-3

CAs act on multiple receptors and ion channels — toxicity is multifaceted:

MechanismClinical Effect
Antimuscarinic (anticholinergic)Mydriasis, dry skin/mucous, hyperthermia, urinary retention, ileus, delirium, hyperreflexia
α₁-adrenergic blockadeVasodilation → orthostatic hypotension, reflex tachycardia
NE reuptake inhibition (early)Initial hypertension, agitation, mydriasis
5-HT reuptake inhibitionSedation, mydriasis, myoclonus, hyperreflexia (serotonin syndrome if combined with serotonergic drug)
Voltage-gated Na⁺ channel block (the killer)QRS widening, wide-complex tachycardia, Brugada pattern, ↓ contractility, ↓ BP
K⁺ channel (rectifier) blockQT prolongation, torsades de pointes, ventricular ectopy
H₁ antagonismSedation, depressed consciousness
📚 Table 177-3 — Pharmacologic Profile of Cyclic Antidepressants (Tintinalli p.1195)
📚 Table 177-2 — Mechanisms for CA Toxicity at Therapeutic Dosages (Tintinalli p.1195)
Inline MCQ 2. Which CA toxicity mechanism is responsible for the wide QRS complex and ventricular dysrhythmias?
A. α-adrenergic blockade
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Antimuscarinic effect
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
C. Voltage-gated Na⁺ channel blockade
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
D. H₁ blockade
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: C. Na-channel blockade — same mechanism as Class IA antiarrhythmics. Treat with sodium bicarbonate. Reference: Table 177-3.

3. Clinical Features

Tintinalli p.1196

Presentation

  • Most fatalities occur within 6 hours of overdose; deterioration can be precipitous in patients who initially appear stable.
  • Anticholinergic toxidrome dominates early: tachycardia, mydriasis, dry warm flushed skin, hyperthermia, urinary retention, ↓ bowel sounds, agitation/confusion.
  • CNS: agitation → confusion → coma; seizures (often brief, generalized); hyperreflexia; myoclonus.
  • Cardiovascular: sinus tachycardia early; wide-QRS tachycardia as toxicity progresses; hypotension; cardiac arrest.
  • Respiratory: depression late; aspiration risk in obtunded patients.
⚠️ Pitfall: An "awake patient with mild tachycardia" can develop seizures, wide-QRS tachycardia, and cardiac arrest within minutes. ALL suspected CA overdoses need continuous cardiac monitoring + serial ECGs + IV access.

Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
D. Dialysis
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: C. CA toxicity may progress rapidly — even reassuring early presentations require ≥6 h monitoring with serial ECGs. Reference: Tintinalli p.1196.

4. Cardiac Toxicity & ECG

Tintinalli Fig 177-1, p.1196–1197

Classic ECG findings

  1. Sinus tachycardia (early, anticholinergic).
  2. Prolonged PR, QRS, QT intervals.
  3. Right axis deviation of the terminal 40 ms of the QRS — most specific finding.
    • Tall R wave in aVR ≥3 mm
    • S wave in I and aVL
    • Or R/S ratio in aVR >0.7
  4. QRS >100 ms → 33% risk of seizures; QRS >160 ms → 50% risk of ventricular dysrhythmias.
  5. Brugada-like pattern may emerge.
  6. Wide-complex tachycardia, torsades de pointes, ventricular fibrillation — late and lethal.
📚 Fig 177-1 — 12-lead ECG showing classic CA toxicity: sinus tachycardia + prolonged PR/QRS/QT + right axis deviation of the terminal 40 ms (Tintinalli p.1197)
"Liebelt criteria" (1995) for predicting risk in suspected CA overdose:
• Limb-lead QRS >100 ms
• R wave in aVR ≥3 mm
• R/S ratio in aVR ≥0.7
Any one criterion → significantly elevated risk of seizures and dysrhythmias.

C. Right axis deviation of the terminal 40 ms QRS / tall R in aVR
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.

Answer: C. Terminal R-wave axis shift to the right (R in aVR ≥3 mm, R/S ≥0.7) is the most specific. Reference: Tintinalli p.1197 + Liebelt criteria.

5. Diagnosis

Tintinalli p.1196
  • Clinical + ECG findings primary; serum levels not used for acute management.
  • Standard urine immunoassay for "TCAs" detects CAs with low sensitivity / specificity. False positives: carbamazepine, cyclobenzaprine, diphenhydramine, quetiapine, phenothiazines.
  • Co-ingestion screen (acetaminophen, salicylate, ethanol) — common in self-poisoning.
  • Labs: ABG/lactate, electrolytes (esp. K⁺), creatinine, CK, β-hCG.
  • Continuous cardiac monitoring; serial ECGs every 1–2 h until stable.

6. Treatment

Tintinalli Table 177-4 p.1197
📚 Table 177-4 — Treatment of Cyclic Antidepressant Overdose (Tintinalli p.1197)

Step-by-step priorities

  1. ABCs — early intubation if obtunded or seizing; protect airway before procedures.
  2. Cardiac monitoring + IV access × 2 + 12-lead ECG (and serial).
  3. Decontamination: activated charcoal 1 g/kg PO if <1 h post-ingestion AND airway protected. Avoid whole-bowel irrigation, multidose charcoal.
  4. Sodium bicarbonate (see next section) for QRS >100 ms, hypotension, dysrhythmias, or acidosis.
  5. Hypotension: isotonic crystalloid 10 mL/kg bolus → if persistent, norepinephrine (preferred — directly reverses α-blockade). Avoid dopamine (less effective; metabolized to NE which is depleted).
  6. Seizures: benzodiazepines first; phenobarbital second. NEVER use phenytoin (Class I antiarrhythmic effect) — worsens cardiac toxicity. NEVER use flumazenil (precipitates seizures).
  7. Hyperthermia: active cooling, sedation.
  8. Replace electrolytes: K⁺ as needed (NaHCO3 will lower K⁺); Mg if torsades.
⚠️ DRUGS TO AVOID in CA toxicity:
• Class I antiarrhythmics (procainamide, lidocaine, flecainide, propafenone) — additive Na-channel blockade.
• β-blockers — worsen hypotension, blunt compensatory tachycardia.
• Calcium channel blockers — worsen hypotension and conduction.
• Phenytoin — Class IB-like effect on Na channels.
• Physostigmine — risk of asystole, seizures.
• Flumazenil — precipitates seizures in mixed-OD.
• Class III (amiodarone, sotalol, ibutilide) — prolong QT further → torsades.

7. Sodium Bicarbonate — The Antidote

Tintinalli Fig 177-2, p.1197–1198

Indications

  • QRS duration >100 ms
  • Wide-complex tachycardia or other ventricular dysrhythmias
  • Hypotension refractory to fluids
  • Metabolic acidosis (pH <7.20 from CA effect)

Dosing

  • Bolus: 1–2 mEq/kg IV push (50–100 mEq for 50 kg adult); repeat every 3–5 min until QRS narrows or pH 7.50–7.55.
  • Infusion: 150 mEq NaHCO3 in 1 L D5W at 1.5 × maintenance; titrate to keep pH 7.50–7.55.
  • Avoid pH >7.55 — alkalosis itself can cause arrhythmias.

Mechanisms of Action

  1. Alkalinization ↓ ionized fraction of CA available to bind Na channel.
  2. Sodium load overcomes Na-channel block by mass action.
  3. Both contribute to QRS narrowing and hemodynamic improvement.
📚 Fig 177-2 — A: wide QRS in amitriptyline overdose. B: same patient, ~3 h after IV bolus NaHCO₃ — QRS markedly narrowed (Tintinalli p.1198)
Side effects: hypokalemia (K⁺ shifts intracellularly with alkalosis), hypernatremia, fluid overload, metabolic alkalosis. Monitor K⁺ q1h initially and replace.

Hypertonic saline alternative

  • If sodium bicarbonate is contraindicated (severe alkalosis already), hypertonic saline (3% NaCl) can provide the sodium load without alkalinizing further.
Inline MCQ 8. A patient with CA overdose has pH 7.55, K⁺ 3.0, QRS 110 ms. Which intervention is most appropriate?
A. Continue NaHCO3 infusion
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
B. Stop NaHCO3 and add hypertonic 3% saline + replace K+
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
C. Stop NaHCO3, give Class I antiarrhythmic
Correct option. Read the full rationale below.
D. Initiate hemodialysis
Incorrect option. Compare against the correct choice and rationale below.
Answer: B. pH already 7.55 — further alkalinization risky. Provide Na load via 3% NaCl + replace hypokalemia. Reference: Tintinalli p.1197."

8. Refractory Cardiotoxicity

Tintinalli p.1198

Step-up therapy when NaHCO3 fails

  1. Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV for refractory dysrhythmias / torsades; overdrive pacing.
  2. Lidocaine 1–1.5 mg/kg IV — paradoxically may help by displacing CA from Na channels (controversial; use cautiously when other measures fail).
  3. IV lipid emulsion (Intralipid 20%) — emerging evidence for severe CA toxicity refractory to standard therapy. Bolus 1.5 mL/kg over 1 min, then infusion.
  4. VA ECMO — case series support survival in refractory cardiogenic shock from CA toxicity.
  5. Glucagon — anecdotal effectiveness for hypotension; 1 mg IV bolus.
Pearl — adjunct therapies are LAST resort: Aggressive sodium bicarbonate + norepinephrine + benzos for seizures + supportive care address the majority of cases. Reach for lipid emulsion and ECMO only when standard care fails.

9. Disposition

Tintinalli p.1196
  • Discharge from ED: asymptomatic patient + normal ECG + no anticholinergic findings × 6 h continuous monitoring + sober + reliable disposition.
  • Admit to telemetry/ICU: any conduction abnormalities, prior altered mental status, sustained tachycardia, anticholinergic features, hypotension, sustained-release preparation, large dose, polypharmacy ingestion, or inability to assure compliance/safe disposition.
  • Psychiatric evaluation mandatory for all intentional ingestions before disposition.

⚕️ ATLS 11th — Toxic Coingestion in Trauma

ATLS — Toxicology / Special Considerations
  • Suspect CA overdose in trauma patients found unconscious with anticholinergic features.
  • ECG should be obtained on every trauma patient with altered mental status — wide QRS may indicate toxic ingestion.
  • Avoid Class I antiarrhythmics (lidocaine for torsades, procainamide) as empiric anti-arrhythmic in undifferentiated trauma if CA OD possible.
  • Sodium bicarbonate is safe to give empirically in suspected CA ingestion with QRS >100 ms even before confirmation.
  • Coordinate poison control consultation early.
Rosen source: Rosen is used to cross-check cyclic antidepressant ECG risk markers, sodium bicarbonate endpoints, seizure control, and refractory shock management. Rosen vs Tintinalli: Tintinalli supplies the core overdose algorithm; Rosen adds bedside pitfalls and escalation triggers.

📗 Rosen's EM 10th — Cyclic Antidepressants

Rosen's Ch.143 (Antidepressants)
  • Aligns with Tintinalli on key principles: ECG-driven management, sodium bicarbonate as foundation antidote, NE for refractory hypotension, benzodiazepines for seizures.
  • Rosen's emphasizes caution with charcoal in patients with depressed mental status due to risk of aspiration — protect airway first.
  • Lipid emulsion therapy — Rosen's lists as level C (case-report) evidence for refractory CA toxicity. Reasonable adjunct when conventional therapy fails.
  • Aggressive ICU monitoring ≥24 h for severe ingestions due to rebound risk.
  • Dialysis is NOT useful (high Vd, high protein binding) — both texts agree.

🔑 Key Points (High-Yield)

  1. CA toxic dose: >1 g (or >15–20 mg/kg) — narrow therapeutic-toxic window.
  2. Toxidrome: anticholinergic + α-block hypotension + Na-channel block (wide QRS) + K-channel block (long QT).
  3. ECG markers: QRS >100 ms (33% seizure risk), R in aVR ≥3 mm, terminal 40 ms right axis deviation.
  4. Sodium bicarbonate = antidote: 1–2 mEq/kg bolus → infusion to pH 7.50–7.55. Mechanism: alkalinization + Na load both help.
  5. Norepinephrine for refractory hypotension (NOT dopamine).
  6. Benzodiazepines for seizures. NEVER phenytoin (Class IB additive), NEVER flumazenil (precipitates seizures), NEVER physostigmine.
  7. Hemodialysis is INEFFECTIVE — high Vd, high protein binding.
  8. Charcoal: single dose if <1 h post-ingestion AND airway protected; otherwise skip.
  9. Avoid Class I antiarrhythmics (procainamide, lidocaine first-line, flecainide), β-blockers, CCBs.
  10. Refractory: Mg, lidocaine cautiously, lipid emulsion, ECMO.
  11. Monitor ≥6 h asymptomatic, telemetry/ICU if any toxicity.
  12. Most fatalities in first 6 h; deterioration may be precipitous in initially well-appearing patients.
